However, it should be noted that correct response rates to question 2 (“In a large-scale disaster, approximately how long does it usually take for local emergency services to assist individual households?”) remained high at both post-tests 1 and 2 (Table 3). Question 2 relates to self-sustainability postdisaster and is a salient concept at the heart of personal preparedness. Pretraining and post-training assessments gauged whether information and tools conveyed during the workshop were associated with an increase in preparedness activities or confidence postworkshop. The number of respondents reporting personal emergency kits and preparedness plans increased immediately after the workshop compared to before the workshop (post-test 1 vs baseline). The first finding may be explained by the distribution of small household preparedness items during the course of the workshop. The latter finding may be explained by an exercise in which participants discussed important components of preparedness and started drafting their plan. One-year postworkshop, the percentage of respondents who reported having personal emergency kits and preparedness plans increased from post-test 1, suggesting some respondents assembled supply kits and plans after completing the workshop (Table 2). At post-test 2, more respondents reported having kits (77.3 percent) than having emergency plans (66.7 percent). This finding is in line with several other studies reporting that people are less likely to create a family plan than assemble a supply kit. 25-28 The percentage of respondents reporting confidence in personal preparedness activities also increased from baseline to post-test 1 and was maintained or increased at post-test 2 (Table 2), suggesting that respondents felt more confident in their personal preparedness knowledge and abilities immediately after and up to 1 year following the workshop. Of the three “get a kit, make a plan, be informed” tasks, “be informed” was the most difficult to quantify. To gain information on the “be informed” activity, two perception comments were used: “confidence in knowing what protective actions to take” and “confidence in knowing where to find more resources and information” (items 7 and 8, Table 2).

Of the three “get a kit, make a plan, be informed” tasks, “be informed” was the most difficult to quantify. To gain information on the “be informed” activity, two perception comments were used: “confidence in knowing what protective actions to take” and “confidence in knowing where to find more resources and information” (items 7 and 8, Table 2). These two comments are a subjective self-assessment and thus do not measure whether the activity was performed. It should also be noted that many emergency planners and academic researchers frame personal disaster preparedness around only two tasks: collecting emergency supplies and creating a preparedness plan. 2,25-28 Although these are the two most frequently observed constituents of personal preparedness activities, the researchers chose to follow the FEMA three-activity personal preparedness model in line with current US federal guidance. Furthermore, the importance of “staying informed” is well established in the professional literature, with several studies supporting the notion that people with higher threat-specific knowledge are more likely to prepare for these events. 26,29,30 More respondents perceived severe personal consequences resulting from a moderate flood (item 3 in Table 4) at post-test 1 compared to baseline and posttest 2. This suggests that information conveyed in the workshop may have increased participants’ threat perception initially; however, it was not retained 1- year postworkshop. Given there were no severe flood events in West Virginia in the year that followed the workshop, threat perception may have also been moderated by an “incident-free” year. Interestingly, respondents who were in their current profession for more than 1 year were more likely to perceive severe consequences resulting from a moderate flood than respondents in their current profession for less than a year. This may indicate increased experience working with floods or a better understanding of the potential consequences of a moderate flood. A sharp decrease in the percentage of respondents who perceived severe public health consequences resulting from a moderate flood in their region (item 2 in Table 4) was observed at post-test 2 as compared to baseline and post-test 1. This indicates a reduced threat perception by participants’ 1-year postworkshop.

A sharp decrease in the percentage of respondents who perceived severe public health consequences resulting from a moderate flood in their region (item 2 in Table 4) was observed at post-test 2 as compared to baseline and post-test 1. This indicates a reduced threat perception by participants’ 1-year postworkshop. Personal preparedness in the context of EPPM theory EPPM theory would suggest that those who fall into a HT/HE category would likely engage in more personal preparedness activities than in the other categories. This finding has also been shown outside the context of EPPM in studies suggesting that higher 

perceived risk is associated with greater rates of personal preparedness activities. 2,5,26,29,31,32 Several of our findings are consistent with the EPPM. HT respondents tended to agree more often that severe personal impacts were likely to result from a moderate flood than LT respondents at post-tests 1 and 2. HE respondents perceived confidence in their knowledge and the impact of their response on their job success at higher rates than LE respondents at all survey administrations. At post-test 1, and to a lesser degree at post-test 2, HE respondents had higher rates of perceiving an impact of their response on overall success than LE respondents. At baseline, HE respondents were more informed than LE respondents about what to include in a family emergency kit and emergency plan, protective actions to take in a disaster, and where to find information on preparedness activities. One-year postcurriculum, the level of self-reported kit-making and confidence in information-acquisition behaviors was at or near 100 percent across all EPPM profiles. The EPPM predicts that personnel fitting HT/HE profiles would consistently be more apt to engage in desired personal preparedness behaviors; however, we cannot evaluate this prediction at post-test 2 when nearly all personnel reported the same behavior. Further qualitative study, along with expanded geographical research beyond a single state, is warranted to gain additional nuanced insights. Facilitators and barriers to preparedness behaviors With respect to factors that could assist participants in completing household preparedness tasks, results suggest employees would benefit from more training on personal preparedness and access to easy instructions and relevant information on undertaking such tasks.

Facilitators and barriers to preparedness behaviors With respect to factors that could assist participants in completing household preparedness tasks, results suggest employees would benefit from more training on personal preparedness and access to easy instructions and relevant information on undertaking such tasks. Lack of time, interest and “buy-in” from family members were mentioned as both barriers and facilitators to performing preparedness behaviors. The issue of time may be simply resolved by LHD employers allocating work hours for completion of specific personal preparedness activities to support overall workforce preparedness. Family cooperation may be improved by periodic family preparedness training or “fun-days” where partners and children are encouraged to attend information sessions and preparedness-focused games—such days could also be promoted as community events. Lack of money was mentioned as an important barrier to completing preparedness tasks deemed “too expensive” such as stocking up on food and purchasing basic preparedness supplies. This barrier has important policy implications especially in West Virginia, one of the lowest income states in the United States. Given local governmental workforce cutbacks amidst fiscal austerity, and the backdrop of a growing array of public health threats, an “all-hands-on-deck” approach to preparedness is crucial. Every LHD employee should have a critical role to play in disaster response. If employees are prepared for emergencies, they are more likely to report to duty knowing their families and homes are secure. A possible solution is government funding earmarked as an investment to ensuring enhanced workforce capacity by encouraging the personal preparedness activities of LHD employees.

Although the “Think Inside the Box Delivery Toolkit” has enabled West Virginia LHD staff to continue delivering personal preparedness trainings, workshops have generally been limited to West Virginia. Baseline, post-test 1, and post-test 2 surveys were anonymous and could not be matched to the same respondent over all survey administrations. Therefore, it was not possible to look for average individual changes over time. The number of respondents within EPPM and demographic categories was not sufficiently large to fit regression models. Hence, we present percentages and p-values to help quantify the associations between these categories and responses to the attitudes/beliefs and personal preparedness questions. Because of the small number of responses within categories and inability to match respondents’ answers across survey administrations, more extensive statistical analyses could not be conducted. The knowledge assessment tool, composed by subject-matter experts to address core concepts of FEMA personal preparedness materials, was neither validated nor verified and test questions were not linked to specific desired competencies.

The ultimate goal of personal disaster preparedness is a well-trained workforce, able to serve a community that is similarly well prepared. It follows that a well-prepared household lessens (but does not necessarily fully eliminate per se) worker distraction created by concern for the safety of family members, apprehension about arriving to work safely, lack of self-efficacy, and a lack of understanding of local public health threats. In the context of the study, personal preparedness was measured through knowledge questions and use of the FEMA three-activity personal preparedness model. Overall, the workshop was well received by participants and successful in increasing engagement in personal preparedness activities, with the percentage of respondents reporting emergency kits, preparedness plans, and confidence in personal preparedness activities all increased at post-test 2 (compared to post-test 1). Although there was a measured surge of knowledge immediately post-workshop there was no significant surge seen one-year post workshop – which may indicate there was no retention of knowledge post workshop. If so, this could identify the need for longitudinal follow-on activities to sustain and reinforce initial gains from personal preparedness trainings. Further, the study illustrates how established behavioral models such as the EPPM can facilitate examination of, and underpin interventions to address, long-recognized gaps in personal disaster preparedness, including among responders themselves. This study not only provides initial insights but also points to still-unanswered questions about the longitudinal relationship between the EPPM’s dimensions of threat and efficacy and desired personal protective behaviors among a centrally important response cadre. Given the importance of personal preparedness from a policy implementation standpoint, future research could explore these critical unanswered questions through expanded cohort analyses and mixed methods designs.

More extreme weather patterns caused by climate change are leading to more intense and frequent flooding in some of the world’s most vulnerable locations. The Republic of South Sudan faces obstacles mitigating rivers and urban floods caused by heavy rainfall in many of its regions. Through a focused review of the related literature, this study will first analyze the effectiveness and failures of the South Sudanese government’s attempts to mitigate flood risks, save lives, and prevent property damage. Study data are derived from various sources including peer-reviewed research, government and nongovernment documents, and the news media. Next, using similar qualitative review methods, a parallel case study from Bangladesh will be used to glean comparative findings and help formulate flood risk reduction recommendations for South Sudan.

Two examples of this smaller scale approach to structural mitigation for DRR can include the Trapbag system and Gabion wall systems. Trapbag systems. TrapBag is a multipurpose system used for flood protection, mudslides, river stabilization, stormwater containment, dams, dikes, levees, seawalls and has a life span of 5 years from the moment of installation. 80 The TrapBag system (Figure  3), which is cost-effective, easy to ship, and store, protects the entire wall from being compromised if one bag fails as the next one will remain strong, keeping the whole barrier working in the same capacity and providing flood protection. 78 This system has been used successfully in several US states experiencing the effects of climate change like Illinois and Florida. 82,83 Referencing Figure 4, several planeloads of these bags were quickly flown to Argentina for water containment in response to the 2011 Valadero Gold Mine cyanide spill, 84,85 which illustrates the potential of this product to be utilized internationally with minimal notice.

Based on the findings of this study and the subsequent discussion, five recommendations were derived as a starting point to developing meaningful, practical, and actionable flood risk reduction strategies in South Sudan including: 1. Establish a flood mitigation strategy that brings together local, state, national, and international organizations to work together under one national policy. This includes building partnerships among profit and non-profit, community-based, and faith-based organizations. 2. Develop local DRR through non-structural emergency management training and education programs. This includes strengthening educational institutions to develop a curriculum for teaching natural disaster awareness, flood risk reduction, disaster planning, preparedness, response, mitigation, and recovery. 3. Develop and enhance regionally supported and locally accessible EWS capabilities as part of non-structural flood mitigation measures and connect this to local emergency evacuation training. 4. Implement structural flood mitigation strategies using simple but accessible methods like the Trapbag or Gabion wall systems. 5. Procure funding through international resources like the World Bank to invest in building nationwide critical infrastructure that includes urban planning, land use, hospitals, roads, building codes, bridges, floodwalls, levees, flood barriers, and dams.

The ongoing conflict, safety concerns, and travel insecurity prohibited interviewing or gathering other empirical data for this study which may have led to, for example, determining the viability of a low-elevation property buyout program as another means of sustainable flood mitigation in South Sudan. However, this study has produced five actionable and practical recommendations as a meaningful starting point for ongoing flood mitigation efforts for this country that is just beginning only its second decade in existence. Opposite the forces of climate change, flooding in South Sudan will be worse in the next decade. Therefore, a focused effort to use structural and nonstructural means to mitigate this ongoing threat to begin to improve local resilience by moving the people of South Sudan away from subsistence living and toward economic resilience is essential. Additionally, predicting flooding events requires adequate resources and technological innovation which is lacking in countries like South Sudan. The Bangladesh case study and disaster risk reduction programs represent a potential path forward for South Sudan for building their disaster risk reduction strategies. South Sudan has more natural resources than Bangladesh 99 but having unified voices among government officials to tackle corruption issues can help prevent resource mismanagement, allow the country to invest in sustainable DRR programs, and save lives. Current flood warning system in Japan and its effectiveness in mobilizing evacuation: Lessons from case studies Guangwei Huang, PhD Juan Fan ABSTRACT An effective flood warning system is crucial for successful flood management. Flood warning systems have been developed in many countries across the world. However, scientific literature on flood warning systems has been mainly focused on technical capacity building, and the effectiveness of warning systems in mobilizing evacuation was much understudied. Japan is a country with a long history of fighting against flood disasters; the evaluation of its practices in providing flood warnings and the effectiveness are certainly important for further flood research development in Japan, and sharing the experience and lessons with the rest of the world will contribute to flood damage reduction on a global scale. Following this line of thinking, this article is intended to present a clear and concise picture of the current flood warning system in Japan, which has been poorly documented up until now. It is also aimed at providing a performance assessment for the flood warning system through case study approach and the use of Strengths, Weaknesses, Opportunities, and Threats (SWOT) model. Through analyses, the pros and cons of the current flood warning system in Japan are highlighted, and the directions for further development and refinement are explained. Key words: flood warning, evacuation, Chikuma River, Kuma River, SWOT INTRODUCTION Flood warning systems are a crucial component of flood disaster management because they can save lives and reduce damage to individual property and social infrastructure. As the population living in flood-prone areas and the value of urban and rural assets exposed to flood risk are growing rapidly due to urbanization and climate change, a better and effective flood early warning system is in high demand. Having such a system enables authorities to take appropriate action such as evacuation instruction and dam or retarding basin operation in advance of a flood event to avoid or minimize catastrophic outcomes when severe weather strikes. In contrast to flood forecasting systems, which assess flood risk, the main purpose of a warning system is to issue warnings when a flood is approaching, imminent, or already becoming a disaster.

Having such a system enables authorities to take appropriate action such as evacuation instruction and dam or retarding basin operation in advance of a flood event to avoid or minimize catastrophic outcomes when severe weather strikes. In contrast to flood forecasting systems, which assess flood risk, the main purpose of a warning system is to issue warnings when a flood is approaching, imminent, or already becoming a disaster. Moreover, the multifunctionality of flood warning systems can also promote and improve community preparedness for flood disasters and increase understanding of risks and appropriate flood responses. Because of its importance, flood warning systems have been established in many places across the world. 1-3 According to a study by Perera, 4 the number of flood early warning systems nearly doubled since 2000. Although many research works on flood warning systems have been conducted from various perspectives during the last two decades, these studies were either conducted for technology development 5-9 or information dissemination-centered and community-focused, 10-12 the actual operation of flood warning system in warning issuance and its effectiveness in mobilizing evacuation have been very much understudied. The current increase in the number and degree of flood disasters makes the further development or refinement of flood warning systems a necessity for establishing a society resilient to climate change. This study employed a mixed methods approach. First, it used document analysis to synthesize technical details for clarifying the state of the art in flood warning and emergency management in Japan. Document analysis is a form of qualitative research in which documents are interpreted by the researcher to give voice and meaning around an assessment topic, 13 and often used in combination with other research methods as a means of triangulation. Target documents of this study are technical reports of the Ministry of Land, Infra-structure, Transport and Tourism (MLIT), and Prefectural and Municipality Governments of Japan. Second, after revealing technical details of the flood warning system in Japan, this work used case study approach to evaluate the overall performance of the current flood warning system in Japan and to gain a better understanding of the direction for further development of the flood warning system. Two cases were chosen in this study. The first is the flooding in the middle reaches of the Chikuma River in 2019, which caused serious damage in the Nagano Prefecture. 14 Chikuma River is the longest and widest river in Japan, flowing through three prefectures: Nagano, Gunma, and Niigata. As it runs from the Nagano Prefecture into the Niigata Prefecture, the waterway is renamed to the Shinano River, and it finally empties into the Sea of Japan. Historical records showed that 26 largescale flood disasters have occurred in the watershed of the Chikuma River from 1742 to 2020, and 11 of them occurred since 1980. 15 In 2019, the levee of the waterway at the Hoyasu location breached, and the inundation resulted in a 974,000,000 JPY loss in the Nagano City. 16 There is a hydrological gauging station (Kuiseke) 25.6 km upstream of the levee breach site, and another one (Tategahana) 5.5 m downstream of the breaching site. Water level monitoring data from 2010 to 2019 from the two stations were analyzed to examine the appropriateness of the warnings issued. This study also collected various information related to evacuation, interviewed 11 local residents in the most damaged area, and conducted a questionnaire survey to identify problems in emergency management with a particular focus on emergency information dissemination among foreigners living in Nagano City.

This study also collected various information related to evacuation, interviewed 11 local residents in the most damaged area, and conducted a questionnaire survey to identify problems in emergency management with a particular focus on emergency information dissemination among foreigners living in Nagano City. The rationale is that it is important to evaluate a flood warning system from both hardware (technical details) and software (convincing people to evacuate). The main questions in the questionnaire survey for non-Japanese residents were: (1) do you speak Japanese, (2) did you receive emergency information and from where, and (3) did you evacuate following emergency calls. For Japanese residents, the questions were: (1) did you receive emergency information and from where, (2) did you evacuate following emergency calls, (3) if yes, the evacuation was carried out by a car or on foot, and (4) if not, what are the reasons. The interview probed into the flood risk perception of residents and asked about their experience in the evacuation process and opinions on emergency management. The second is the flooding of the Kuma River in 2020, which caused serious damage in Hitoyoshi City, Nagano Prefecture. The Kuma River is the longest river in the Kyushu region of Japan and known as one of the three most rapid rivers of Japan. Eleven major flood disasters occurred in the watershed since 1927 according to the Kyushu Disaster Database. 17 In 2020, a torrential rain caused levee breaches and overflows at multiple locations in Hitoyoshi City. The flood disaster claimed several dozens of lives and inundated 7,400 houses. 18 There are two hydrological gauging stations in the most affected area, so that the water level data of the two stations were analyzed to evaluate the warning system in this river. It also collected various information related to evacuation and conducted questionnaire survey for problem identification like the first case. For the two cases, field inspections were conducted at locations where levee breach occurred, and questionnaire surveys were carried out in both Nagano City and Hitoyoshi City for further problem identification. Flood warning system in Japan Document analysis revealed that Japan has a five-stage flood warning system at present, which is based on information on heavy rainfall from the Japan Meteorological Agency (JMA) and hydrological monitoring stations. 19 It provides municipalities with criteria to issue emergency response instruction of different level. The structural details are compiled in Table 1, which are little known to scientific communities outside of Japan. In the system, Level 1 is an early warning issued by the JMA for the possibility of heavy rain. Level 2 warning is also issued by the JMA for heavy rain and flooding alert. Level 3 indicates that danger is approaching, and the warning is issued by municipalities. At this stage, the elderly and disabled should start evacuation, while others prepare for evacuation. Level 4 indicates the need for a full evacuation. Level 5 signifies the occurrence of disaster and the need to take whatever action is necessary to safeguard one’s own life. In implementing this system, a technical question is how to determine each level. Currently, the criterion is the river water level. 20 Each warning level is associated with a water level in the river channel. Particularly important are the so-called evacuation judgment water level and the flood danger water level. Once evacuation judgment water level is reached, local government should issue evacuation instruction to the elderly and disabled. As water level rises from evacuation judgment water level to flood danger water level, evacuation instruction will be issued to all in risky areas. In theory, the determination of the two water levels should be based on records of the water level rising rate at the gauging site to provide sufficient lead time to all, especially the elderly and disabled to prepare for evacuation. However, the actual setting of evacuation judgment water level and flood danger water level has not been well documented, and its effectiveness in mobilizing evacuation has not been evaluated so far. According to the Basic Act on Disaster Management of Japan established in 1961, municipalities can direct residents for evacuation in the case of emergency and are responsible for preparing regional Disaster Prevention Plans, which includes criteria for issuance of evacuation information, and implementing it as well.

This is because the term “advisories” gave residents a misperception about the need of evacuation. As a matter of fact, flood evacuation rates in Japan were quite low. 21 During the flood disaster in the Hiroshima Prefecture in 2018, local governments issued evacuation instructions to the total number of 329,203 people. However, the records of shelter use showed a total of 9,489 people went to 145 shelters in the prefecture. This indicates that the evacuation rate was as low as 2.8 percent. To improve evacuation, the use of evacuation advisories was abandoned, and evacuation instruction is issued at the time previously set for evacuation advisories. Since water level is used to issue warnings of different level, the key for the system to function properly is the scientific soundness of the determination of the evacuation judgment water level and the flood danger water level. Document analysis also found that at present, all rivers in Japan are classified into three categories, 22 namely, rivers with flood forecast, rivers with the provision of water level information, and rivers with flood alert. Rivers with flood forecast are rivers flowing through two or more prefectures or rivers with large basin areas that are likely to cause serious damage to the national economy if they overflow. Rivers with the provision of water level information are relatively small rivers, in which water level may increase too fast to predict with sufficient lead time.

For a designated cross-section, we use the water level rising data to find a water level that can provide a 60-minute lead time before it rises to the levee height. SWOT analysis is a structured planning method that evaluates those four elements of an organization, project or business venture. Because it is a simple, but powerful framework for leveraging the organization’s strengths, improving weaknesses, minimizing threats, and taking the greatest possible advantage of opportunities, this study employed SWOT analysis to discuss how to move forward with the cur - rent flood warning system in Japan. Too large a lead time might lower alert level of residents. Such a psychological factor has been poorly considered in evacuation planning so far. According to the John Leach’s disaster psychology theory, there are three phases in human behavior in relation to disasters: before, during, and after the impact of disaster. Before the impact, people are aware of the coming impact but try to ignore or deny the facts, reducing uneasy feelings of danger and showing apathetic behavior with respect to the real danger. Therefore, a large lead time could become an excuse for residents not to act quickly or take the wrong action as revealed in the study. It is hypothesized here that the relationship between evacuation rate and lead time takes an inverse U-shape. As lead time increases, evacuation rate will increase at first and then decrease once the lead time reaches its turning point. This turning point is the optimal lead time, and its determination is critical for better emergency management. Furthermore, evacuation-aiding capacity should be built up together with flood forecasting capacity. A flood warning system without emergency response capacity will not function effectively, no matter how accurate and reliable the warning system is. A fundamental issue is that disaster resilience is frequently pursued separately by the public and private sectors. Building public–private partnerships to enhance emergency capacity is a key for disaster reduction.

This study uses FEMA’s new flood model software, HAZUS-MH (Multi-Hazard), to assess the socio economic damages following floods. HAZUS-MH provides dollar figures for land use planners, flood managers, and emergency planners to utilize in their preand post-disaster planning of the economical, social, and environmental consequences of flooding. HAZUS-MH estimates financial losses resulting from a 100-year flood by analyzing the potential direct and indirect economic damages that could occur in a local jurisdiction. HAZUS-MH Flood Model and Hurricane Wind Model was used to estimate losses in the Parish of East Baton Rouge, Louisiana, as part of the jurisdiction’s hazard mitigation planning process. Depth grid maps and flood loss maps are explained and displayed to show the results of the flood hazard and loss analysis. The article evaluates HAZUS-MH against the criteria of quality, timeliness, and completeness. The different levels of HAZUS-MH are explained within the context of accuracy. The article also explains how geographic information system (GIS) data layers can be made available to public officials by use of a free downloadable GIS data reader.

Causing an average of $5 billion in damage each year, floods are the most chronic and costly natural hazard in the United States. 1 Despite advances in flood science and progress in the implementation of federal hazard reduction policies, financial damage from flooding continues to escalate. 2 The Worldwatch Institute determined that floods are responsible for half of all deaths worldwide from natural disasters. Between 1985 and 1999 economic losses from flooding accounted for roughly 28 percent of total global economic losses. 3 Although North America suffered a relatively low percentage, (only 1 percent) of the world’s natural disaster-related deaths for this interim, flood Hazard mitigation planning utilizing the HAZUS-MH Flood Model and Hurricane Wind Model John C. Emergency management has utilized hazard maps for some time to clarify the nature and extent of flooding and wind hazards. The Tennessee Valley Authority (TVA) and the US Army Corps of Engi - neers (USACE) were early leaders in the initiative to characterize the nature of floods and understand their impact. Congress authorized the National Flood Insurance Program in 1968 with the enactment of the National Flood Insurance Act, which was administered by the US Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD). 4 Flood insurance rate maps (FIRMs) provide a visible illustration of the geographic extent of flooding. By showing base elevation requirements, FIRMs make further information available on the hazard. In January 2004, FEMA released HAZUS-MH (Multi-Hazard), a new emergency planning and re sponse software package. The HAZUS-MH mapping and modeling software utilizes the power of geographic information systems (GIS) and hazard modeling to estimate associat- ed social and economic losses as well as characterize the nature and extent of flood, wind, and coastal hazards. This paper provides an illustration of how a local community used HAZUS-MH to assess and reduce the direct and indirect social, economic, and environmental losses from flood hazards. The latest version of HAZUS-MH extends natural hazard modeling from a single focus on earthquake hazards to a multihazard analysis system including earthquake, flood, and wind hazards. HAZUS-MH helps emergency managers to determine the potential damage from inland and coastal flooding, hurricane winds, earthquakes, and chemical hazards. 5 Local, state, and federal officials can improve community emergency preparedness, response, recovery, and mitigation activities by enhancing the ability to characterize the economic and social consequences from flood, wind, and coastal hazards. 6 Officials at all levels of government have long recognized the need to more accurately estimate the escalating costs associated with natural hazards. 4 The Hazard Mitigation Act of 2000 requires that local jurisdictions complete a comprehensive analysis as a part of their hazard mitigation plan in order to qualify for FEMA mitigation funds. The basic analysis uses USGS Digital Elevation Model (DEM) surface grids and discharge frequency values from either the National Flood Frequency Program or,when available, USGS gauge stations. The advanced anal ysis uses either USGS DEM surface grids or higher resolution DEMs from Light Detection and Ranging (LIDAR). Advanced flood modeling in HAZUS-MH utilizes hydraulic analysis from the USGS Hydrologic Engineering Center River Analysis System (HEC- RAS). As required for a basic analysis, users conducting an advanced analysis must identify a flood study area and obtain a USGS DEM for the area. A USGS Web site link within HAZUS-MH provides the pathway to a USGS mosaic of 30-meter DEMs and 10- meter quads specific to the study area. The mosaic is in a GRID file format and reflects the surface elevations throughout the study region. Outputs from the advanced analysis using HEC- RAS are the same as the basic analysis; the depth grid, however, is determined from an engineering hydraulic analysis rather than the general statistical discharge estimates reflected in the National Flood Frequency Program (NNF) or values from the USGS HEC-RAS. Depth is determined for a specific flooding event by comparing the flood elevation along a water feature with the land surface elevations as denoted in the GRID file. Flood elevations for specific cross sections of the water feature are determined using HEC-RAS. The initial input into the East Baton Rouge Hazard Mitigation Program was a HAZUS-MH basic flood analysis. This type of general analysis renders a foundation for an assessment of the nature and extent of flooding in a study area. The damage calculations reflected in the basic flood analysis help form a general comparison among regions in the study area. Because the parish was divided into seven major drainage areas, the estimated losses to structures and their contents may be compared among drainage areas. This analysis establishes a baseline for prioritizing future analyses using the advanced features of HAZUS-MH and HEC-RAS. East Baton Rouge Parish anticipates utilizing advanced flood analysis capabilities of HAZUS-MH by incorporating previous HEC-RAS into the program.

Local and state emergency management (EM) directors have many legal duties. These duties are based on specific EM law and other laws of general application, such as Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) law, contract law, personnel law, and government ethics law. They also have the responsibility for purchasing systems and equipment that best meet the needs of their departments while staying within the confines of time and budget. This article will present guidelines for successfully negotiating EM contracts. State emergency management law Every state has some form of EM law. Such laws typically relate to: n setting up a state emergency or disaster management agency, n specifying state and local organization roles in responding to disasters, n assigning executive authority to declare a state of emergency, n explaining special executive powers that result from such a declaration, n allowing cooperation in the form of mutu- al aid with neighboring jurisdictions, n drafting emergency plans and keeping them current, n compiling and distributing a list of emergency duties for all officials, and n documenting the chain of command for continuity of government purposes. State EM statutes often address other aspects of disaster preparedness and response, assigning a broad and varying set of responsibilities to emergency managers. For example, in Indiana, emergency managers fulfill a variety of duties during all phases of EM and are also responsible for preparing and keeping emergency plans current, preparing and distributing a list of emergency duties for all officials, and documenting the chain of command for continuity of government purposes. The definition of “emergency management” lays out the broad scope of the discipline’s responsibilities. In a general sense, it relates to the preparation for and coordination of all emergency functions other than those designated to military forces or other federal agencies to prevent, minimize, and repair injury and damage resulting from disasters. The basics of contract law are straightforward, consisting of three elements: 1. the offer; e.g., “I will sell you these goods or perform these services for this amount of money”; 2. acceptance; and 3. consideration (the fee paid for the services). To facilitate mutual understanding, contracts are typically written rather than oral. A written agreement allows both parties to see clearly the subject matter of their bargain. Difficulties arise when the parties do not have a mutual understanding of exactly what is offered or the nature and character of the consideration. One key thing to remember is that the party that initially drafts the contract will typically end up with a document reflecting his or her desires more than those of the other party. This is why emergency managers should, whenever possible and particularly with expensive purchases, see that their attorney drafts the contract. For some, this step is a given, as many units of government have standardized contracts for purchase of goods or services. Another tack is to take the contractor’s document and use pieces of it in crafting one’s own contract. Frequently, though, contractors have standard contracts of their own that they will submit as the first draft. They may say that they always use this contract and threaten to walk if it is not used. In such cases, it is not a bad idea to let the contractor walk away from the deal. Remember, for the most part the purchaser has the upper hand in negotiations, because he or she has the money, and the contractor needs the work to prosper. Sometimes, the contract officer will be tempted to use the contractor’s document as is, because it means less work for that busy individual. One must be extremely careful in reviewing such texts and be ready to delete unacceptable language. These documents are often worded to contain indemnification requirements, waivers of inadequate performance, arbitration clauses, and other language that dilutes the obligations of the contractor. They may also include requirements that are contrary to state or local law. The emergency manager and his or her attorney or contract officer should carefully scrutinize the contents of standardized contracts, particularly when bigticket items are involved. Modification of standard language is often in order in such situations.

Modification of standard language is often in order in such situations. Performance standards One key part of drafting a contract for purchase of goods is performance standards. These are particularly important when the items purchased are being custom built. The emergency manager and the field expert need to get together to discuss in detail exactly what is desired and how it is expected to operate when installed. They then need to meet with the attorney or contracting officer to make sure the standards are written into the contract in complete form. If this preparatory step is proper- ly taken, the emergency manager is much more likely to end up with the end product desired. Sidestepping political pressure in awarding contracts When purchasing a complex and expensive system, there may be political pressure to award different contracts to various people within the jurisdiction with the goal of “spreading the wealth.” Although this may sound like a good idea, in actuality it could be the cause of unending headaches. When a system such as a communications network is installed, all of its parts must work together properly for it to perform as advertised. If multiple contractors perform the work, they may all point fingers at one another if there is a problem and refuse to cooperate and address it. This can be expensive and politically embarrassing. One good way to avoid this problem is to insist on a turnkey system with guarantees in the contract that it will perform as advertised prior to acceptance by the purchaser. To help ensure this, it is important to set up a schedule of partial payments that holds back a significant portion (typically 25 to 33 percent) until verification tests, possibly by a third party, have been performed to ensure the entire system functions properly. When the actual product differs from the contents of a written contract, the party whose expectations are frustrated will have a number of legal options. First, there may be a cause of action for damages or specific performance. Second, the contract may be repudiated or cancelled.

ABSTRACT
Resilience refers to the capacity to withstand, overcome, or recover from serious threat, such as a natural disaster. In small towns, community leaders are intimately involved with their towns’ response and recovery from a disaster and can see resilience processes, or their absence, virtually one person at a time. The authors interviewed 30 community leaders in two small towns along the Red River of the North, 7 to 8 years after a devastating flood. Responses to the question, “Based on your experience and observations (in your community), what advice would you give a similar community that was trying to recover from a major flood?” revealed a pattern of suggestions consistent with resilience strategies identified in the psychological literature. Specifically, the strategies of taking action, accepting help from others, engaging in self-discovery, maintaining a realistic long-term perspective, and fostering hope and optimism were mentioned repeatedly by the respondents. The authors also found rich subthemes within each of these general strategies. These findings support the applicability of psychological resilience strategies to a community’s disaster response and recovery processes.

resilience, recovery, leaders, rural INTRODUCTION Natural disasters such as floods stress communities in a number of ways. They may cause damage to private and public property and disrupt basic and necessary community services (eg, emergency services and electric power). How well a community recovers from a flood depends partially on the magnitude of disaster-related loss and the extent to which lost resources can be replaced and remaining resources applied to the work of recovery and rebuilding. 1 Recovery from a major disaster may be particularly stressful for small rural communities because of the limited financial and personnel resources available. Resilience involves the ability to “bounce back” from difficult experiences, such as a natural disaster, and to produce positive outcomes in spite of stressful circumstances. 2,3 Psychological theorists and researchers have conceptualized resilience in various ways: a set of stress-protective factors and attributes, a process of developing skills and strategies to cope with adversity, and a motivational force that contributes to personal growth through adversity. 4 Although the majority of studies in psychology on resilience have focused on individual characteristics and behaviors, the psychological concept of resilience can be extended to apply to a community’s effort to recover from a disaster. 5 In this article, we apply principles of resilience to understanding the responses of community leaders who were asked, following a 500-year flood experience, to give advice to other communities facing major disasters. The American Psychological Association 2 (APA) published a list of 10 ways to build resilience, which includes both behavioral and cognitive strategies. The recommended behavioral tools include social support, goal setting, taking decisive action, and self-care. Cognitive strategies include various forms of cognitive reframing (ie, seeing the crisis as manageable, accepting change as a normal part of living, and taking a longterm perspective), discovery of one’s strengths and weaknesses, building self-confidence, and fostering Strategies for resilience: A qualitative analysis of rural community leaders’ advice on disaster recovery George A. Youngs, Jr., PhD H. Katherine O’Neill, PhD JEM

hope and optimism. Decisions about which resilience strategies are used in a given situation are influenced by personal characteristics, learning history, and current environmental conditions. Overall, the process of building resilience requires persistent effort and flexibility in adapting to changing circumstances over time. 2 Models of resilience that delineate specific factors and strategies provide a way of studying how individuals respond to stressful situations. We propose that these models may also provide a useful heuristic for understanding community disaster response and recovery efforts. The purpose of this study is to determine the extent to which community leaders’ advice on how best to respond and recover from disaster reflects the resilience strategies described in the psychological literature.

Community selection This study is part of a larger project that is studying two US communities impacted by the 1997 Red River Flood. The Red River’s watershed begins in southern Minnesota with its headwaters near the border communities of Wahpeton, ND, and Breckenridge, MN. The Red River then gently meanders north along the border between North Dakota and Minnesota, crosses the US-Canadian border, and then continues further north through the city of Winnipeg, Manitoba. The Red River’s route creates the Red River Valley, but it takes a perceptive eye to see anything resembling a valley in the basin’s prairie flatland. When this otherwise modest river floods, it really floods, spreading across miles of farmland and into the hearts of many river-edge communities. With very few topographical features to stop its flooding waters, even small Red River floods can be major events, but the 1997 Red River Flood exceeded the River’s predesignated 500-year flood level. The 1997 flood triggered one of the largest ever, pre-Katrina city evacuations. Citizens of Grand Forks, ND, on the Red River’s west bank and Grand Forks’ sister city, East Grand Forks, MN, on the Red River’s east bank had to “get out of town fast” when the flood waters topped their opposing levees. Considerable press attention— local to international—was given to the dramatic evacuation of these twin cities with the penultimate attention grabber of a Presidential visit. Still, there was much more to the story. The raging Red River ravished the entire river valley with many heroic flood battles occurring both south and north of the “Grand cities,” but in smaller communities and with much less attention. We chose to focus our research efforts on the flood battles of two small towns, Breckenridge, MN, and Drayton, ND. Breckenridge is a community of nearly 4,000, whereas Drayton is just under 1,000. Both of the communities are on the Red River, but they had very dissimilar flood experiences. Despite a ferocious battle, much of Breckenridge was inundated by the 1997 flood. In contrast, Drayton stayed dry behind an improvised dike that engineers said would not work, but did. Selecting smaller communities such as Breckenridge and Drayton enabled us to identify and interview many, if not most, of the key community leaders in these towns’ distinctive flood fights.

Interviewee selection We interviewed 15 citizens in Breckenridge and another 15 in Drayton. With approval of the Institutional Review Board at North Dakota State University, Fargo, we constructed appropriate consent forms indicating to respondents our desire to talk about “community perceptions and values and how these relate to your town’s recovery over the last several years from the 1997 flood.” We said that the purpose of the study was “to help communities and agencies guide people through the recovery process . . . .” Finally, we told interviewees that “you have been selected because we believe your experiences and perceptions will enhance our understanding of your community.” Our primary goal was to focus on individuals dealing with community recovery processes; therefore, we selected interviewees who were and are in positions that give them a community-wide perspective. We began by contacting individuals with visible leadership roles. We then expanded our list by asking at the end of each interview “Is there anyone else you know who we should interview as part of this project?” As a result of these efforts, we spoke with a variety of community leaders including city council members, active mem- bers of various nonprofit organizations, business leaders, and religious leaders, as well as selected community citizens, outside the leadership structure, who were directly affected by the flood (eg, lost their home or business). All participants agreed to have their interviews recorded digitally and/or on audiotape. The interviews generally lasted for an hour and an half and were conducted in a variety of locations from homes, to business establishments, to the local cafe. The interview team included both the authors and three trained graduate student research assistants. We conducted these interviews throughout 2004 and 2005, roughly 7 to 8 years after the 1997 flood. Despite this considerable lapse of time, citizens told us that the flood was still a frequent topic of conversation because of the historic magnitude of the event and the ongoing community mitigation efforts triggered by the 1997 flood. Questions All interviews followed a structured guide with over 40 open-ended questions. Each question was read out loud and, if needed, followed by prompts, such as, “Could you tell me more?” The focal question for this study was the following: “Based on your experience and observations in Breckenridge/Drayton, what advice would you give a similar community that was trying to recover from a major flood?” This question was located near the end of the survey. It came after a series of questions requesting interviewees to reflect on their community’s losses and gains associated with the flood. Thus, respondents had thoroughly discussed their own community’s experiences by the time respondents were asked to give advice to others. Coding Each interview was transcribed and coded. Coding Each interview was transcribed and coded. For the aforementioned question, we began, as noted earlier, with an a priori coding scheme based on the 10 resilience strategies listed by APA. 2 To improve coding reliability, we reduced the 10 strategies to six categories by combining similar strategies together. Specifically, we combined two action-based strategies (ie, goal-setting and taking action toward goals) into a category labeled “taking action.” We combined three cognitive reframing strategies (ie, seeing the crisis as manageable, accepting change as a normal part of living, and taking a long-term perspective) into one category which we labeled “taking a realistic perspective.” We also combined building self-confidence and holding a hopeful, optimistic view of the future into a single category labeled “foster hope and optimism.” Thus, our a priori categories consisted of the following resilience strategies: (1) take action; (2) accept support and help from others; (3) engage in self-discovery; (4) maintain a realistic perspective; and (5) foster hope and optimism. We found that these categories easily fit the data and covered virtually all of the interviewees’ comments. However, we also initially included a sixth strategy from the APA list, self-care, that barely surfaced in respondents’ comments—a point we will discuss at the conclusion of the article. For now, we turn to our results for our five combined APA resilience strategies. Maintain a realistic perspective Another type of advice that community leaders gave was to admonish other communities to have a realistic view of the long-term nature of disaster recovery. For the most part, this involved encouragement to be patient. Several interviewees focused on task patience, that is, the need to recognize how long it takes to complete recovery tasks. Others focused on emotional patience. To these interviewees, it was important to tell individuals in another community that there will be light at the end of the tunnel. Task patience. “What I can tell you is that if you think it’s going to be over quickly, if you think you’re going to bounce back quickly, it’s not going to happen. Many of our interviewees offered hope to fellow communities dealing with disaster. These statements of hope took several forms, from general optimism to focusing on specific projects and people, such as rebuilding a “new” town, engaging in mitigation efforts, and ultimately, trusting the wisdom and dedication of community leaders. It’s almost as if interviewees are telling others, “You should hope that things will be better—maybe, I think.” In the face of a major disaster, hope appears to be a fragile emotion.

When asked to offer advice to another community facing disaster, our interviewees were ready to do so. Take action. Seek help. Discover your strengths and weaknesses. Be patient. Hope. These are the suggestions that come from the literature on resilience, and they are the suggestions that are clearly echoed by our interviewees. So, what have we learned? First, these suggestions are not just platitudes. They come from people who have been on the front line of a major disaster. There is an emotional intensity in some of the comments similar to what one might hear in the voice of a parent pleading with a child to listen and learn life’s lessons before it is too late. Second, there is an inner richness to be found in these simple suggestions. Take action means something very specific to these interviewees. It means coordinate, clean-up, do the paperwork, listen to experts, and do it right. Seek help means set aside your pride and make connections. Self-discovery is both practical and philosophical—learn about your community’s resources, learn about your community’s vulnerability, and learn about your community’s character. Be patient means be patient with everything, emotions, projects, and people. Hope means hope for the future, but also do not lose faith. It is the inner richness of these resilience suggestions that makes them come alive for communities facing disaster in the future. Third, the emphasis that interviewees placed on taking action and seeking help provides a road map for outside experts who wish to offer help. Community leaders want help and appreciate the need for outside expertise. They also know that they have to do the paperwork necessary to get expert help—they have to jump through the hoops. These comments all suggest that outside experts will be welcomed and respected. However, it is also clear that outside experts are expected to jump through some hoops as well. They need to respect how hard it is to ask for help. They also need to provide real help. If you are going to help, bring real resources and a willingness to take action yourself. An outsider’s expertise will be respected if it is demonstrated rather than flaunted. Fourth, the strategies of resilience are a means to an end.

They need to respect how hard it is to ask for help. They also need to provide real help. If you are going to help, bring real resources and a willingness to take action yourself. An outsider’s expertise will be respected if it is demonstrated rather than flaunted. Fourth, the strategies of resilience are a means to an end. Taking decisive action, maintaining a realistic perspective, and other strategies are methods by which communities can restore damaged resources and protect against future loss. Many of the community leaders’ comments had to do with obtaining knowledge and accessing funds to fuel recovery efforts. For example, the resilience strategy of accepting help is used to obtain expert advice on how to access emergency funds to repair homes and public structures, and the strategy of maintaining a realistic perspective (ie, having patience) is applied toward the goal of pursuing longterm mitigation projects. Findings of this study fit well with the literature on community disaster recovery. In a landmark study, Rubin et al. 9 studied communities recovering from major disasters, focusing specifically on decisions made by public officials and their impact on the recovery process. They identified three essential elements for timely and cost-effective community recovery: personal leadership, the ability to act, and knowledge of what to do. Our findings are consistent with those of Rubin and colleagues in several important ways. First, town leaders embraced the personal qualities of resilience and applied them to leadership of the community at large. Second, our respondents repeatedly emphasized the importance of taking action, including administrative action (eg, doing necessary paperwork) and obtaining needed resources (eg, federal assistance). Finally, community leaders recognized the need for information about how to respond to the disaster and sought expert advice to supplement their own experience in dealing with hazards such as flooding. Future research needs to examine resilience and recovery over the long term. Research on long-term disaster effects supports the notion that replacing lost resources is important to recovery. Hobfoll et al. 10 suggest that, in the wake of disaster, basic practical and physical needs must first be met to foster community 

recovery and protect against long-term psychological distress.

recovery and protect against long-term psychological distress. The emotional reactions of children and adults to disaster have been linked to several aspects of the recovery environment (eg, social support, financial assistance, and restoration of community services). Persistent disaster-related disruptions in home and work environments can have a negative impact on family functioning and may contribute to higher rates of depression, anxiety, anger, and suicidality. 11 Arata et al. 12 found significant emotional and physical distress among fishermen who had experienced deterioration in social relationships and persistent financial losses secondary to a catastrophic oil spill 6 years earlier. Mitigation efforts may serve to enhance personal and community resilience against future disaster events by protecting vital resources and enhancing community cohesion. 10 Presumably, the resilience strategies offered by our community leaders, including taking action and seeking help, should promote the successful replacement of lost resources, the maintenance of social support linkages, and effective mitigation efforts. Our next research effort— already underway—will be to explore the 10-year impact of the flood on community citizens in Breckenridge through a random sample of respondents and the inclusion of multiple measures of net loss/gain from the 1997 flood as well as measures of current well being. A final observation about the advice given by community leaders is the relative lack of recommendations for self-care. In fact, only two comments among the dozens collected across 30 interviews reflected this concept. Because we did not specifically ask about the use of each resilience strategy, we can only speculate about reasons why self-care was not emphasized. One possibility is that, for small towns facing a major flood, the demands of the crisis were too great to allow community leaders to take time for rest and relaxation. Community leaders were under pressure to work long and hard to protect the town against the flood threat and to aid citizens in the recovery process once the floodwaters had receded.

One possibility is that, for small towns facing a major flood, the demands of the crisis were too great to allow community leaders to take time for rest and relaxation. Community leaders were under pressure to work long and hard to protect the town against the flood threat and to aid citizens in the recovery process once the floodwaters had receded. In fact, had the leaders and residents of Drayton not engaged in a frantic, roundthe-clock effort to construct a temporary dike, they might very well have lost their town to the floodwaters. During a prolonged recovery process, community leaders are charged with planning, funding, and carrying out rebuilding and mitigation projects, in addition to the normal responsibilities of their offices. Community leaders and residents are forced to sacrifice personal wellbeing for the survival of the community under such circumstances. However, the neglect of self-care comes at a high cost. Many of the comments about accepting emotional support from others, having patience with the recovery process, and holding onto a seemingly fragile hope in the future reflect a sense of weariness brought about by the prolonged stress of disaster recovery. So, if we may conclude with our own bit of advice to community leaders facing disaster, please add self-care as much as realistically possible to the remaining resilience strategies advocated by those who have already faced disaster.

ABSTRACT
Objective: Agent-based modeling can provide powerful tools to inform flood emergency management and to provide an assessment of loss of life due to a flood event. The objective of this work is to study the suitability and robustness of this type of models for being applied in practice in managing flood emergencies. Design: This article describes the application of a prototype, agent-based Life Safety Model (LSM) to two populated areas in the Thames Estuary. Parameters sensitivity analyses have also been performed to assess the robustness and the applicability of this model as part of the actual emergency practice.

The model of the two areas resulted in the estimation of the number of fatalities for each scenario for different causes such as drowning, exhaustion, building collapse, and vehicles being swept away. The model was also successfully validated against historical data from the 1953 Canvey Island flood. Conclusions: The LSM offers a scientifically robust method of assessing injuries and lives lost, and it allows the comparison of different emergency management strategies that could assist in reducing the loss of life during future flood incidents. Key words: flood, disaster management, emergency planning, loss of life, agent based INTRODUCTION An accurate understanding of loss of life and injuries as a flood event unfolds is valuable for developing and improving emergency plans for areas at risk. Despite the global impacts of floods, there are a limited number of methods to estimate the loss of life and the evacuation times for flood events. Loss of life modeling can be performed at different levels of detail as follows:  Macro or overall event level , where one mortality rate is applied to the whole of the exposed population.  Meso or group/zone level , where mortality rates are estimated for groups of people or specific zones.  Micro or individual level , where the circumstances and behavior of each individual is modeled to estimate each person’s probability of dying. Until recently, most of the loss of life models for floods were based on a statistical analysis of fatalities and injuries from historical events to date. In the United Kingdom, the work done to assess the loss of life and evacuation times for flood risk areas has been limited to macro- or meso-level estimates. The “Risk to People” model, developed as part of a Department for the Environment Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) research project, is the most commonly used tool in the United Kingdom to assess flood fatalities. 1 However, this meso-level method is based on an empirical, generalized model that does not use detailed information on each individual in its “broad-scale” estimates of loss of life.

Empirical methods do not represent, at a detailed level, the many attributes (eg, age and health) that are important determinants of loss of life.  Evacuation is not considered as a separate process, and the benefits of those who move to safe havens are often not explicitly included.  The effectiveness and rates at which the flood warning message is disseminated are not taken into account. Empirically based loss of life models tend to apply one mortality rate to an area and do not take into account the cause of death. Jonkman analyzed 13 flood events in Europe and in the United States that resulted in 247 reported flood-related fatalities. Each event occurred in the past 20 years and involved relatively few deaths. Jonkman considered events to be representative for extreme events in most Western European countries. 2 Drowning accounted for some 67 percent fatalities. Vehicle-related casualties for drowning were found to occur most frequently as a result of people attempting to drive across flooded bridges, roads, or rivers. Physical traumas account for 12 percent of the fatalities, most of which occurred while people were in their vehicles. Physical traumas account for 12 percent of the fatalities, most of which occurred while people were in their vehicles. Other causes of death included heart attacks during evacuation and return, electrocution during clean up, and deaths from fires following a floods. To provide a more accurate assessment of loss of life and evacuation times, an agent-based model is required. An agent-based model is a computational model that simulates the interactions of autonomous receptors with a view to assess their effects on the system as a whole. It can model the simultaneous operations of multiple “agents” or receptors (in this case, people and vehicles) with the floodwater, in an attempt to re-create and predict the actions of complex phenomena such as those that occur in flood emergency. The modeling of the evacuation process generated by an approaching flood is included within such a model. This is important for those responsible for flood event management planning. It can identify “bottlenecks” in the escape network before they are experienced in an evacuation, it can also be used to determine the impact of road closures due to flooding, the impact of phased evacuation on traffic loading, and many other possible consequences of an evacuation event. In the United Kingdom, there has been little work undertaken for evacuation modeling specifically for flood event management. The objective of this work is to study the suitability and robustness of agent-based models for being applied in practice in managing flood emergencies. In particular, this article describes the application of a recently developed, agent-based, microlevel Life Safety Model (LSM). This work was undertaken as part of Task 17 of the European Community funded research project FLOODsite. 3 Rather than relying on very scarce and possibly unrepresentative observations on life loss caused by large floods, the LSM is designed to generate insightful information about this complex phenomenon by observing the simulated behavior of a physically based virtual representation of the inundation area and its inhabitants as they mobilize to escape flooding.

THE BC HYDRO LIFE SAFETY MODEL Background The LSM is a piece of prototype software developed by BC Hydro in Canada that previously had only been used to carry out dam break risk assessments for small communities (eg, less than 3,000 people) in Canada. The LSM allows dynamic interaction 

between the receptors (eg, people, vehicles, and buildings) and the flood hazard. The LSM requires a significant amount of data including:  the location of individual properties, vehicles, and people;  flood depths and velocities from a twodimensional hydrodynamic model of the flood event; and  details of the road network and other pathways. Figure 1 provides a conceptual view of the architecture of the LSM. The core of the system is the LSM Simulator that requires two inputs: an initial state of the world (which describes modeling receptors such as people, buildings, cars, and roads) and the flood wave. The simulator output includes an estimated loss of life and dynamic computer graphics visualizations. The system models the “fate” of a set of receptors, which are described by their position at each time step through the simulation. Each receptor can have a set of properties that describes its normal location/ condition during a week, such as travel times, school/ work hours, and weekend activities. Other timevarying properties include the ability of the people, vehicles, and buildings (ie, the receptors) to withstand the effect of the floodwater. The LSM also models how people would react to the approaching wave, with and without a formal evacuation warning.

Before any loss-life-modeling can be carried out, the following has to be undertaken:  Two-dimensional hydrodynamic modeling of the flood area to produce a temporal varying of grid of depth and velocity.  A “virtual world” needs to be set up representing the initial state of the world before the flood occurs. The representation of the population at risk and their associated vehicles, buildings, and other infrastructures are encompassed in what is termed a “People’s World.” The various features that input to and affect on this world, such as the flood wave and the flood warning systems, are realized via a set of submodels that can collectively operate on the People’s World. Figure 2 shows representation of the People’s World in the LSM. At the beginning of a simulation, all the people at risk are either located in a building or in a vehicle on the road network. A number of different People’s Worlds can be set up depending on the time of day, day of the week, and the time of the year. The LSM uses a generalized event logic to determine the location of each person, whether they are aware of the flood wave, whether they are trying to find a safe haven, what happens if they encounter the flood, and whether they survive or not. A loss function related to each receptor (eg people, buildings, and vehicles) specifies the ability of a receptor to resist the impact from the flood wave, in terms of depth and velocity, and how these can change during an event. There can be instantaneous loss when an individual encounters with fast-flowing water, a group who has sought safety in a building can suffer cumulative loss if the building collapses, or a slow deterioration in health if they are exposed to the flood water for a significant length of time, as a result of hunger or cold. As a flood event evolves, the interaction of receptors with the flood wave will impact the ultimate loss of life.

APPLICATION OF THE LSM TO CANVEY ISLAND Background Canvey Island, shown in Figure 4, is an island in the Thames Estuary, covering an area of 18.5 km 2 . The mean high water mark of the Thames Estuary at Canvey Island is higher than most of Canvey Island’s land. The first sea defenses were constructed in 1623, and the Dutch settlers formed the first Canvey Island communities of the modern era. The population did not expand rapidly until the 1920s, with 1,795 inhabitants in 1921, but the population expanded more than 6,000 in 1927. In the latter period, the number of buildings rose from 300 to about 1,950. 7 In 2001, its population was estimated to be approximately 37,000. 8 In 1953, the island was inundated by the “Great North Sea Flood” that breached flood defenses and resulted in the deaths of 58 people and the destruction of several thousand houses. 9 The likelihood of flooding of the access routes to and from Canvey Island will increase following the rise in sea level. Access to Canvey Island is currently possible only by two roads, both of which are connected to the same roundabout. Any disruption to these routes would hamper evacuation and severely limit access.

However, it has been found that while substantial, these defenses show signs of deterioration such as cracks in the concrete and the degradation of seals between slabs. 9 Although the current standard of protection at Canvey Island is of 0.1 percent (1 in 1,000 years), this will be reduced to 0.5 percent (1 in 200 years) by 2030 owing to the rise in sea level and the subsidence affecting the south of the United Kingdom. In Canvey Island, it has been estimated that 30 percent of properties are bungalows and 45 percent of Figure 4. Locations of Canvey Island and Thamesmead.

The readily available data for Canvey Island comprised the following:  Population data were available from the Office for National Statistics at an output area level. Output areas contain an average of around 125 houses.  Number of vehicles at an output area level is available from census data.  Topographic data in the Thames Estuary LIDAR survey data were available with a vertical accuracy of approximately  25 mm.  The locations of properties were available in the form of a national property dataset that provides geo-referenced details of each of the properties in England and Wales.  The road network was digitized from street and Ordnance Survey maps. These data were used to construct a “virtual” representation of the modeled areas that were used by the LSM. The majority of the effort expended in the work was related to setting up the virtual representation of the areas of interest. Hydrodynamic modeling of the 1953 flood To model the 1953 Canvey Island flood, a historical analysis was undertaken to reconstruct the situation that existed at that time. Important sources of information included historical maps of the island, articles from 1953 newspapers, books, 7 police reports, and the results of physical modeling carried out in 1954. This information was used to assist in assessing the height and location of the 1953 flood defenses, to update the digital terrain model, to reconstruct the tidal shape, and to assess the incoming flood volume associated with the breaches that occurred. The modeling technique used here is finite difference model provided by the software TUFLOW. Being a finite difference modeling, the domain has been discretized in a regular 20-m grid, covering the total domain with an area of 18 km 2 . The time span of the model is 8 hours. The results of the hydrodynamic model indicated that the 1953 flood covered most of the Canvey Island. The model showed that the water depth was 3 to 4 m at the point closest to the breach with a mean depth of between 0.8 and 1.0 m. The modeled volume of the 1953 flood was estimated to be 12.6 million m 3 .

The BC Hydro LSM model indicated that approximately 100 to 120 fatalities had occurred during the 1953 event. This number is dependent on the “resilience factors” applied to both people and buildings. The actual number of people who died in 1953 was 58. The number of buildings destroyed during the event is unclear. However, the available anecdotal evidence seems to be similar to the LSM model results in the order of magnitude, even if this number of destroyed building in the LSM seems to be overestimated. Figure 5 shows the results of the loss of life modeling using the LSM for the 1953 flood. Of the 13,000 people living in the island in 1953, the model indicated that there would be 119 fatalities, 48 as a result of drowning and 71 as a result of exhaustion. The LSM also indicated that some 2,300 would be “toppled” (ie, knocked over) by the floodwater. This 

figure can be used as a proxy for the number of injuries that are likely to occur. Parameter sensitivity analysis The 1953 Canvey Island modeling has been a good workbench to test the sensitivity of the model to the variation of the model’s parameters. Rate of warning. In the model, the velocity of the alarm dissemination, starting from the warning center, can be set up. This parameter states the rate of the warning spreading out from the warning center in the radial way. The model is sensitive to the variation of this parameter. It has been noted that the number of deceased people is 10 times bigger if the parameter is divided by three, but it also obviously depend on other parameters such as the position of the warning center. Therefore, the sensitivity in this parameter is fully justified with the analysis of the real world.
